deep.reconstruction:
The page has three blocks. All are about the integral logarithm li(e^x) = Ei(x) and its divergent asymptotic series. In Gauss's notation Πn = n!.

(A) Number table (top). Read the rows as power series in t = 1/x^2 (or 1/u^2):
 a = 1 - 2t + 24t^2 - 720t^3 + ... = Σ (-1)^k (2k)! t^k
 b = 1 - 6t + 120t^2 - 5040t^3 + ... = Σ (-1)^k (2k+1)! t^k
Taking termwise differences:
 c = a - b = 0 + 4t - 96t^2 + 4320t^3 - 64·5040 t^4 ...
Here the coefficient of t^k is (-1)^{k+1} 2k·(2k)!, i.e. 3!-2! = 4, 5!-4! = 96, 7!-6! = 4320, 9!-8! = 322560 = 64·5040.
The next row is
 d = 4b - c (factor 4 chosen to kill the leading term after dropping the vanishing constant) = 72t - 3840t^2 + 302400t^3 - ...
Check: 4·6 - 96 = -72, 4·120 - 4320 = -3840, 4·5040 - 322560 = -302400, up to the overall sign convention.
The last line is
 e = 18c - d, where 18 = 72/4 again kills the leading term. [Mine:] this gives e = 2112t^2 - 224640t^3 + ...

This is Euler's 'reduce by successive remainders' process, i.e. a Euclidean algorithm on power series. It turns the ratio of the two series into a continued fraction [mine]:
 a/b = 1 + 4t/(1 + 18t/(1 + (88/3)t/(1 + ...))).
Why these two series [mine]: a and b are exactly the imaginary and real parts of the asymptotic series of Ei at an imaginary argument. From e^{iu} Σ k!/(iu)^{k+1}, the bracket equals -i·a/u - b/u^2 with t = 1/u^2. So a and b are the asymptotic series of the auxiliary functions of the sine and cosine integrals. Gauss stops at e; the next partial quotient 88/3 is not an integer, which may be why.

(B) Gauss writes the truncated asymptotic series
 li(e^x) ≈ e^x(1/x + 1/x^2 + 2/x^3 + ... + Πn/x^{n+1}).
He puts x = r(cosφ + i sinφ), so e^x = e^{r cosφ}(cos(r sinφ) + i sin(r sinφ)). He notes r sinφ = π/2, the case where the oscillating factor becomes purely imaginary. 'li. iu' plausibly means li of an imaginary argument iu. This links (B) to the table (A). The small triangle sketch presumably depicts r, φ.

(C) Remainder at optimal truncation. Gauss defines P(n) = ∫_{-∞}^{n} e^x x^{-n} dx = ∫ e^{x - n log x} dx.
The exponent x - n log x is stationary exactly at x = n. Also the remainder of the li-series after the term (n-1)!/x^n is (n-1)!-type times ∫_{-∞}^{x} e^t t^{-n} dt. So taking the upper limit equal to n means studying the remainder at the point where the series' terms are smallest (optimal truncation).
He sketches a rectangle-rule approximation ω{e^n/n^n + e^{n+ω}/(n+ω)^n + e^{n+2ω}/... }.
He then differentiates under the integral sign, including the variable upper limit (Leibniz rule):
 ∂P/∂n = -∫ log x · e^x x^{-n} dx + e^n/n^n.
Writing the boundary term as ∫_{-∞}^{n} d/dx(e^x x^{-n}) dx = ∫ (e^x/x^n - n e^x/x^{n+1}) dx, he combines everything into
 ∂P/∂n = ∫_{-∞}^{n} [(x-n) - x log x]/x^{n+1} · e^x dx.
The page ends there.
errors: c = a - b only holds after dropping the zero constant term. d = 4b - c and e = 18c - d silently align the series so that leading terms cancel (a one-step shift). Correct as an elimination scheme, but not literal termwise identities of the written rows.

P = ∫_{-∞}^{n} e^x x^{-n} dx is ill-defined as written for real x. The path crosses x = 0, where x^{-n} is non-integrable for n ≥ 1, and x^{-n} is multivalued for x < 0 with non-integer n. A principal value or complex path (as for Ei) is implicitly needed; Gauss does not address this.
In ∂P/∂n the boundary term is written e^x/x^n; it should be evaluated at x = n, i.e. e^n/n^n. This is a notational slip only.
The ω-sum is an unfinished quadrature sketch: the third term 'e' is cut off, and no step size or error is specified.

results.what: Termwise elimination turning the ratio of the even/odd parts of Σ(-1)^k k! t^k (asymptotic series of Ei(iu)) into a continued fraction: a/b = 1 + 4t/(1 + 18t/(1 + ...))
results.modern_name: Continued fraction (Stieltjes/Euler-type) conversion of a divergent asymptotic series; Euclidean algorithm on power series
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (De seriebus divergentibus, 1760) for Σ(-1)^n n! x^n; Laguerre (1879) and Stieltjes (1894) for Ei / sine-cosine integral continued fractions

results.what: Asymptotic expansion li(e^x) ~ e^x Σ_{k=0}^{n} k!/x^{k+1}, evaluated at complex x = r e^{iφ}
results.modern_name: Asymptotic expansion of the exponential integral Ei / logarithmic integral

results.what: Remainder integral ∫_{-∞}^{n} e^x x^{-n} dx with upper limit at the stationary point x = n of x - n log x (optimal truncation), plus its derivative in n via the Leibniz rule
results.modern_name: Remainder at optimal truncation / converging factor of the li asymptotic series; saddle-point location
results.usually_credited_to: Stieltjes (1886, 'Recherches sur quelques séries semi-convergentes'), later Airey (1937) on converging factors

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's interest in li and its asymptotic series is well known from his letters to Encke and his prime-counting work. Converting divergent series into continued fractions goes back to Euler. The mildly notable point is the deliberate study of the remainder integral with upper limit at the stationary point x = n (optimal truncation), combined with the imaginary-argument series (sine/cosine-integral auxiliaries). This anticipates in outline Stieltjes' 1886 analysis, but it is only a fragmentary set-up with no result.

checkable.asserts: The coefficients of c = a - b are (-1)^{k+1} 2k (2k)!: 0, 4, 96, 4320, 322560.
The fourth entry of row c, 64·5040, equals 9! - 8!.
The row d = 4b - c (shifted) has magnitudes 0, 72, 3840, 302400 with alternating signs, matching Gauss's 72 - 3840 + 302400.

e^{r e^{iφ}} = e^{r cos φ}(cos(r sin φ) + i sin(r sin φ)).
The exponent x - n log x of the integrand is stationary at x = n, the chosen upper limit.
The final combined integrand for dP/dn: d/dx(e^x x^{-n}) - log x · e^x x^{-n} = ((x-n) - x log x) e^x / x^{n+1}.
∂/∂n (e^x x^{-n}) = -log x · e^x x^{-n}, the first term of dP/dn (the Leibniz rule adds the boundary term e^n/n^n).

transcription_corrections: The struck symbol after e^{r cos φ} looks like a crossed-out '4' or '+'; the intended expression is the product e^{r cos φ}(cos(r sin φ) + i sin(r sin φ)).
The trailing '+ e' in the ω-line is the beginning of a third quadrature term (presumably e^{n+2ω}/(n+2ω)^n), not a standalone e.
'li. iu' plausibly means li(iu), the integral logarithm of an imaginary argument; the reading is uncertain.
In the ∂P/∂n line the boundary term e^x/x^n should be read as evaluated at x = n.
